label: No Reasonable Suspicion for the Initial Stop
motion_heading: The Initial Stop Was Not Supported by Reasonable Suspicion

review_conditions.display_note: If the dispute is that the conduct isn't actually a violation, expect the prosecution to argue the officer made a reasonable mistake of law, which can still support a stop (Heien v. North Carolina, 574 U.S. 54 (2014)). Be ready to show the statute is clear and the officer's reading wasn't reasonable.
You aren't sure yet whether the stop's basis holds up. This section was drafted anyway; get the dash-cam footage, the officer's report, and dispatch records before filing, or cut this section.

rule_statements.text: Stopping an automobile and detaining its occupants is a seizure under the Fourth Amendment.
A passenger is seized by a traffic stop just as the driver is, and may challenge the stop's legality.
An officer may not stop a vehicle without at least articulable and reasonable suspicion that the driver or an occupant is subject to seizure for a violation of law.
Reasonable suspicion requires a particularized and objective basis for suspecting the particular person stopped of wrongdoing.
An officer's inchoate and unparticularized suspicion or hunch is not enough.
Presence in an area of expected criminal activity, standing alone, does not supply reasonable suspicion.
An anonymous tip that lacks indicia of reliability does not, by itself, supply reasonable suspicion.

practice_notes: Get the dash-cam and body-cam footage and compare it to the report — whether the claimed violation actually happened is often visible on video.
The stop's lawfulness is judged by what the officer knew before the stop. Facts learned afterward (smell, admissions, contraband) can't justify it retroactively.
If the stop falls, everything that followed (observations, statements, search results) is potentially fruit — consider which later issues depend on it.
